sections.text: य एनं वेत्ति हन्तारं यश्चैनं मन्यते हतम्।
He who thinks that the Spirit kills, and he who thinks of It as killed, are both ignorant. The Spirit kills not, nor is It killed.
It was not born; It will never die, nor once having been, can It cease to be. Unborn, Eternal, Ever-enduring, yet Most Ancient, the Spirit dies not when the body is dead.
He who knows the Spirit as Indestructible, Immortal, Unborn, Always-the-Same, how should he kill or cause to be killed?

We had been discussing Chapter 2, Sankhya Yoga, Yoga of Knowledge. And as we have seen, this is a self unfoldment for the one who has not understood himself. Arjuna has not realized the reality of his own self.
Therefore all this confusion. So rather than just giving him a temporary advice of what is right at this time, help to dispel his myth about the nature of the self and give him the right knowledge. So the verse 11 onwards, we had been discussing the nature of this self.
And the first thing we have heard from Bhagavan is that the self which you and I considered mortal is actually immortal. That the first declaration very bold. We dont find it very bold because we grew up with it.
It was somewhat embedded in our psyche. However, if you imagine your own experiences of your life and your own viewpoint towards life, its extremely revealing. It is completely different than all my experiences so far.
All my life I consider this life to be mortal. Therefore theres fear of death. And now Bhagavan says this life is immortal.
Your self which considers you as you. That which makes me feel I. That feeling I, which is not related to this body, not this mind, not this intellect.
Therefore I always say my body, my mind, my intellect, that entity he calls this mind is, Bhagavan says eternal is imperishable. Thats the first declaration. The second, as we have seen, is the explanation of what this mortal life is all about.
How does it relate to that immortality? He said the immortal self keeps taking different states of existence as the embodied one. Just as within this body there are changes occurring, when this body becomes no longer useful for that embodied one, he moves on to find another body. That change is no different than my growing from baby to young man to old man and then dying.
So the idea or the concept of reincarnation is introduced right away in the second verse of that discourse. Now this is something we do find very controversial. Used to say, One thing good about my profession is I can bluff all my life and never have to prove anything, and nobody can catch me. Thats because this is nothing you can prove objectively -- it is a subjective science.
Subjectively, it can be proved. All our sages and all the prophets of the world have time and again confirmed the nature of this self. But it cannot be transferred that knowledge to you in an objective manner.
Therefore it is called self unfoldment. Therefore it can only be prescribed how to feel it, how to experience it. If I had been to Hawaii and I can give you all kind of explanation, I can write all kind of essays.
But the only way will experience it when you yourself go to Hawaii. So therefore this knowledge can only be experienced. So the concept of reincarnation can only be inferred by our experiences and cannot be experienced or proven objectively in the scientific sense.
And as we had discussed, all of us do come into this world with very different backgrounds, situations and circumstances. And if Bhagavan was all compassionate and equal to all of us, he probably would have created a standard situation for all of us to come in -- same set of parents, same situation, everybody given the same amount of money upfront, and now go do whatever you need to do. But that does not happen.
That does suggest that we may have been carrying some baggage from before we started this journey. I may be carrying some abilities before I started this journey. So it neatly ties together the observations we have in this world -- different people having different abilities right from birth, different tendencies -- suggesting that they must have had different experiences prior to this existence.
So the diversity of situations for all the newly born in this world is somewhat explained by this concept of reincarnation. The third question is: why do I then feel this sorrow and happiness in this world? If my self is immortal, why am I not experiencing it? And it is explained by Matraha Sparsha Tu Kaunteya -- the senses, when they come in contact with sense objects, depending on the sensitivity of the senses, make me feel either pain or pleasure. All these experiences, whether painful or pleasurable, are time-bound and finite.
Therefore, you bear them or enjoy them, but know that they are going to pass. So that explains our situation and how to deal with this life. And then Bhagavan came to the conclusion: Naasato Vidyate Bhavaha.
That which is unreal has no existence. It may be the figment of my imagination. In my perception there is an existence a snake which I am seeing in a rope.
In a classical example, snake does have real existence for the one who is seeing the snake. But in reality the snake has no existence. Because it is asat before my delusion and after my delusion is over.
That snake has no existence. Therefore it is asat that is impermanent. No real existence, but a perceived existence that has no real existence.
There is no being for the unreal to come into existence. And for the real there is no non existence. The real, which is myself, has no question of non existence.
Therefore I say, there was never a time when this king were not there or you were not there. That I in I and you in you and he in him and see in her always existed will exist. Bhagavan said in a different form.
Gold continues to exist; the form continues to change. The form of a gold bar is temporary. At the whim of the owner or the whim of the artist, the goldsmith, that will change and that is impermanent and.
And therefore it does not have a real existence. What is real is the gold existence. So we learned that that which is real never cease to exist.
That which is unreal truly have no existence other than in my perception. This room space truly has no existence other than its own conditioning. There is nothing called room space really exist here other than the space exists here.
But I create room space in my perception because of the walls, floor and ceiling. The mortality is for this walls, floor and ceiling. I can remove them anytime I want as an owner.
Or somebody may decide to destroy it for other reason. But that can never change the nature of the space within this space was here, is here and will be here. So for the spaces perspective, there is no mortality from the conditioning perspective.
It never really had any real existence other than a relative reality. So therefore, Bhagavan says, avinasi tu tadviddhi iena sarvam idam tatam by which this entire Jagat is pervaded. There is existence everywhere.
I exist, you exist, she exists, he exists, chair exists, tree exists. So everything where we see, we consider it in existence. That existence in its purity is all pervading.
Everywhere I see there is some existence of something that all pervading existence. Bhagavan says Avinashi is indestructible. A form of an existence can be destroyed.
Existence itself cannot be destroyed. A table can be destroyed, but the material of the table will remain in some form. Craig is trying to make a table out of now.
The table does not exist right now other than his imagination. But the wood does exist because he said, I have this. I Will buy this and do that that would exist.
Table only exist in his imagination. But with his imagination he can bring the form into existence. And it will exist as long as its time is.
And then somebody will say, this is not good enough and it will be destroyed. So the form has the mortality, not the existence itself. Know that the all pervading self which makes all the existence possible is indestructible.
That also does not exclude you and I. You and I are part of this ever existing, all pervading being. And we have in detail, seen in self unfoldment and thought about.
This body is nothing but the food modified. It was something else. It became food for me, it became my body.
It will become food for some other entities, creatures, worms, whatever, or fertilizer. Because Hindus get cremated. So it will be fertilized.
Vinasam avya yasyasya nakastyan kartum arhati. There is none who is capable of destroying this imperishable self. No matter how much force I can apply to this building.
I can have bulldozers, I can destroy this building, but cannot destroy the space. Space was here, is and will be here. None has any capability to destroy this space.
Because this space is all pervading, ever pervading. No one has any capability to destroy the space. The self in me, Bhagavan said, is similarly imperishable.
And therefore no one has the capability to destroy that. So if you consider I can destroy somebodys self, you are mistaken. Or somebody thinks they can destroy myself, they are mistaken.
Therefore, Gandhiji said, you probably can destroy my body, but you will never be able to win over my soul. Somebody can kill you, but you cannot kill the self in you, the ideals in you. The message which you leave behind.
Nityasya uktaha sharirnaha. So what is destructible? These bodies of this embodied one is destructible as an end. This conditioning of this unconditioned space is destructible.
Space which is all pervading, ever existing, remaining as is. But it has taken up this conditioning, this conditioning which I see as room space is destructible. And it has its own end.
It is own beginning and own end. Therefore, there is a little plaque in every office building or new commercial building. Say create and such, such and such occupancy, such and such.
It says when it was created it does not have a death date. But we know for sure that this building will not be here 500 years from now mortgage companies have figured out the life of your building, typically 30 years. Therefore they give you 30 year mortgage.
Because average life of a building in this country we consider 30 years. So by the time you depreciate the building at the end of 30 years, the value is zero. Now I have to reconstruct what we call it is a adaptive reuse.
And we spent as much money, not as much, probably more money than it took them to build that building and just completely change it into something new warehouse before. Now Im creating office building into it. But it will never exist in the same fashion forever.
It continues to change. For that imperishable ones bodies has end. This conditioning of the room we have said is room, walls, floor and ceiling.
In my case it is my body, mind and intellect. They have end but not the self. Those are the conditioning taken upon by the imperishable self.
Anasi Nah or pramayashya. But that entity which you consider yourself, I consider myself. And he, she herself is Anashinaha indestructible, a prameyashya also incomprehensible.
Thats the problem we have. We just cannot comprehend the self without its conditioning. Imagining a space without conditioning is impossible.
No architect can imagine or no designer can imagine a space. So for me to consider a space, I have to create conditioning in my mind. Therefore, even to conceive the space outside, I can only imagine it in reference to something -- the building across the parking lot, the trees, the sky.
Space itself cannot be grasped by the mind without some conditioning.

These verses deliver a startling truth: He who thinks that the Spirit kills, and he who thinks of It as killed, are both ignorant. The Spirit kills not, nor is It killed. This challenges our fundamental assumptions about death and violence. The eternal Self cannot be the doer of any action, including killing, nor can it be the recipient of any action, including being killed. Actions happen at the level of body-mind-intellect, not at the level of the true Self.
Verse 20 is one of the most quoted descriptions of the Self: It was not born; It will never die, nor once having been, can It cease to be. Unborn, Eternal, Ever-enduring, yet Most Ancient, the Spirit dies not when the body is dead. Notice the paradox: the Self is both eternal and most ancient - it transcends time altogether. And verse 21 poses the logical question: He who knows the Spirit as Indestructible, Immortal, Unborn, Always-the-Same, how should he kill or cause to be killed?
Today, contemplate this: If your true Self was never born and will never die, what exactly do you fear when you fear death? The body will certainly perish - but that is not you. The mind will dissolve - but that is not you either. Try this exercise: imagine yourself as the space within a room. The walls can be painted, damaged, or demolished, but the space itself is untouched. You are like that space - forms come and go within you, but you remain unchanged. How does identifying with this unchanging Self rather than the changing body-mind alter your relationship with mortality?
